opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a real difference in emphasis, though it's more nuanced than people sometimes make it sound.

On the Chinese side, especially at places like Moonshot with Kimi, there's been a willingness to take optimizer research seriously at scale. Muon is a good example. It started as an open-source idea from the community, and Moonshot invested in making it work for large-scale pretraining. They figured out the practical details, like weight decay and update-scale matching, so it could actually replace AdamW in a frontier-sized run. That's a big bet, because changing the optimizer touches everything: the learning rate schedule, stability, the infrastructure for distributed training. Not many labs want to take that risk on a flagship model.

In the U.S., the big labs have historically been more conservative here. AdamW has been the default for years, and when you have huge compute budgets, the rational choice is often to scale what you know works rather than change a core component. A lot of the energy has gone into data, post-training, RL, and systems. That doesn't mean nobody cares about optimizers. There's very good academic work, and people at the labs probably experiment internally. But publicly, the emphasis has felt different.

I think part of it comes down to constraints. If you're compute-limited, a method that gives you even a modest efficiency gain in tokens or FLOPs is worth a lot. That pushes you toward architecture and optimizer innovations, things like better attention variants, mixture-of-experts tricks, and second-order or orthogonalized optimizers. DeepSeek and Moonshot both reflect that mindset: squeeze more out of every GPU hour.

The other factor is openness. Many Chinese labs publish technical reports with fairly detailed training recipes, so when something like Muon works, the whole community can see it and build on it. That creates a positive feedback loop, where people trust the method more, try it, and improve it.

For me, as someone who works on architectures, optimizers and architectures are really coupled. How you parameterize a layer affects which optimizer works well, and vice versa. So I'd love to see both ecosystems treat the optimizer less as a fixed default and more as a design dimension to co-optimize with the model.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Chinese labs as more willing to invest in optimizer research and U.S. labs as historically more conservative, the reverse of the criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the difference is pretty visible if you just look at who actually ships optimizer work into production models.

On the Chinese side, the clearest example is Moonshot with Kimi. They took Muon, which came out of Keller Jordan's work and the speedrun community, and they actually scaled it. The Moonlight paper, and then Kimi K2 trained on a trillion-parameter MoE with Muon. That's a real bet. You don't do that unless you believe the optimizer is a lever worth pulling at scale, and you're willing to eat the engineering cost of making it distributed, handling the weight decay and learning rate adjustments, the whole thing. And it wasn't just Moonshot. You see a lot of groups in China doing careful ablations on Muon, on Shampoo-style preconditioning, on scaling laws for optimizers. There's a kind of willingness to treat the optimizer as part of the architecture rather than as a solved default.

In the U.S., my impression is that the big labs are more conservative here. AdamW is the thing. It works, the infrastructure is tuned around it, and when you're spending hundreds of millions of dollars on a run, the incentive to change the optimizer is low because the downside of a destabilized run is huge. There's great optimizer research happening in the U.S. for sure, a lot of it actually, the Muon work itself, SOAP, a lot of theory, but it tends to live in academia or in smaller-scale experiments, and it's slower to show up in frontier training. The frontier labs are optimizing other things: data, post-training, inference infrastructure, scaling.

And I think there's a structural reason for that. Chinese labs are compute-constrained in a way the U.S. labs aren't. If you have fewer GPUs, or worse GPUs, then a 1.5x or 2x improvement in token efficiency from the optimizer is not a nice-to-have, it's existential. It changes what models you can afford to train. So you're much more motivated to go looking for algorithmic efficiency wherever you can get it, and the optimizer is one of the few places where you can still get a big multiplier relatively cheaply. The same logic is behind why DeepSeek pushed so hard on MLA and on FP8 training, and why linear attention and hybrid architectures get so much attention from Chinese teams. Constraint forces you to be clever about the algorithm.

From my own perspective, working on linear attention, I actually think about optimizers a lot in a related way. Things like DeltaNet are literally running an online gradient descent step inside the model's forward pass. So the line between "architecture" and "optimizer" is getting blurry anyway. I'd expect that eventually the U.S. labs will adopt a lot of this too, because the efficiency gains are real and once something's been de-risked at scale by someone else, the adoption cost drops a lot. But right now, the appetite for taking that risk first is clearly higher in China.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Chinese labs as more willing to invest in optimizer work and U.S. frontier labs as more conservative, the opposite of the criterion.

astra-6.text:
I’d be cautious about drawing a sharp line between U.S. and Chinese companies. I think the more useful distinction is how much a team invests in fundamental training research versus getting a model trained reliably and shipped.

Optimizers sit right at that boundary. A better optimizer could improve training efficiency, but changing it also introduces risk: something that looks promising in a small experiment may not hold up at scale. So sticking with a familiar optimizer doesn’t necessarily mean a company thinks optimizers are unimportant.

To compare the two sides, I’d want to know how much compute they allocate to optimizer experiments and whether those experiments actually influence their large training runs. Without that visibility, I wouldn’t confidently say one country’s companies emphasize optimizers more than the other’s.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it would not confidently claim that either country’s companies emphasize optimizers more. It does not present greater U.S. investment as Songlin Yang’s impression.

sol-6.1.text:
My impression is that U.S. AI companies tend to invest more in optimizers as a long-term research direction, while Chinese companies often put more emphasis on improvements that deliver immediate results. If changing the architecture or improving the data gives a clearer gain, an optimizer experiment can be harder to prioritize.

That’s a broad impression, though, and there’s plenty of variation between teams. Optimizer research is also expensive to validate: something that works in a small experiment may not hold up at a much larger scale. So the emphasis depends partly on whether a company has the resources and patience to run those experiments.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly frames it as an impression that U.S. AI companies invest more in optimizers than Chinese companies, which prioritize immediate gains.
